newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity trades higher on summer demand.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity trades higher on summer demand.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were trading up Monday after backing off morning highs on expected summer cooling demand, industry sources said.

"We moving out of the shoulder and into the head," said one New York-based futures trader, refering to the movement into heavier power demand summer months from lower demand "shoulder" or spring months.
"You're not going to see (prices) coming down in May when the basis is moving up in June," the trader said.

As of 1230 EDT, May Palo Verde (PV) was trading up 50 cents at $16.15 per megawatt hour (MWh) after exchanges in a range of $15.90-16.30, while June was up 30 cents at $16.85 after trade in a range of $16.80-17.00 per MWh.
May California Oregon Border (COB) was trading up 54 cents at $12.60 after exchanges in a range of $12.50-13.00, while June was up 30 cents at $12.30 from trade in a range of $12.25-12.50 per MWh.
Some early futures strength was seen from an unexpected weekend outage at the 1,073 megawatt (MW) Diablo Canyon nuclear unit 2 on the central California coast.

But traders said the outage was short-term, and was having little impact on futures. Pacific Gas & Electric said that the unit was operating at 90 percent of capacity as of early Monday and was expected to reach full production today.
NYMEX said that as of 1215 EDT an estimated total of 118 COB and 110 PV contracts had traded.
Other Western units remained off line, including the 1,080 MW San Onofre nuclear unit 3 in southern California, which was taken down over the weekend for refueling and maintenance.
Planned and unplanned outages at a number of coal-fired generating units in the West were said to be keeping more than 5,100 MW of generating capacity off line.
Traders said summer cooling demand was expected to continue to give power futures support over the next several days.
"Frankly, I think some of these months are a good buy right now," one trader said.

Separately, hydroelectric supplies in the Northwest were said to have tightened in recent weeks as colder-than-normal weather slowed the rate of snowmelt and reduced the amount of runoff into the hydroelectric system.
The Northwest was forecast to have mild weather this week, with readings averaging four to eight degrees Fahrenheit above normal regionwide.
In the Southwest, temperatures were called to run eight degrees above normal in the northwest area and five degrees below normal in the southeast section.
COB open interest for April 11 rose 122 to 4,057 while PV open interest rose 139 to 4,601, NYMEX said.
